Twelve Cores, Two L3s

The memory architecture of the course machine, drawn as blocks. Every capacity is read from /sys and every latency from a measurement, so this is the machine rather than a generic picture of a cache hierarchy — and the two last-level caches really are different sizes.

AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 · Zen 5 12 cores / 24 threads 64-byte lines throughout LPDDR5X 14 GB

01The same caches, drawn to scale

The diagram above is a schematic: every box is whatever size fits. This one is not. Each cache is drawn with its area proportional to its capacity and its distance from the core proportional to its latency — both on ordinary linear scales, with no logarithm anywhere.

DRAM is why the page ends

Main memory holds 305,000× what L1 holds. On this scale its block would be about 11,000 pixels across and would start 2,255 pixels off the right-hand edge. If the L1 square were 5 mm wide on your screen, DRAM would be 2.8 metres across, starting half a metre away. It also breaks the square-root relationship the three caches follow — 553× wider but only 130× further — because it is not on the chip at all, and the distance stops being about crossing an array.

02How to read the block diagram

  1. 1

    Split at L1, unified below

    L1 is two separate caches, because instruction fetch and data access happen at the same time and would otherwise fight for the same ports. From L2 down, one cache holds both.

  2. 2

    Private above, shared below

    L1 and L2 belong to one core. L3 belongs to a complex. Main memory belongs to everybody. The line between private and shared is where coherence traffic starts, and it sits between L2 and L3.

  3. 3

    The two L3s are not the same size

    16 MB for the first 4 cores, 8 MB for the other 8 — 4 MB per core against 1 MB per core. A working set that fits in L3 on one core can miss to DRAM on another, which is why any measurement here is pinned.

  4. 4

    Everything moves in 64-byte lines

    Every arrow in the diagram carries a whole line, never a byte. That single fact is most of what makes an access pattern fast or slow — see One Core’s View.

Where the numbers come from

Capacities, associativity, set counts and line size are read from /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cache/. Latencies come from a randomised pointer chase (cache_latency.c), pinned and warmed, so nothing is prefetched and the figure is the real cost of reaching that level.

This page is generated by make_block_diagram.py — run make page to rebuild it. Nothing here is hand-typed, so the diagram cannot drift from the machine it describes.
